title: Chapter 223 – The Ones Who Said No
html:
[Hall of Ten Thousand Names – Cheng Hui]

Cheng Hui has outlived three wives, two wars, and the belief that a man can be exact about anything, and on the morning the sleepers begin to wake he is sitting in the east annex with a cold cup of tea and a stack of ledgers, doing the one thing he has always done best, which is to count what cannot be counted.

He is eighty-three years old. He is thin, and dry, and bent at the shoulder like a heron, with a long pale face and a scholar's stoop and a manner so exact that the young clerks in the Hall of Ten Thousand Names have a saying about it: if Master Cheng says it is half past nine, check your watch against the sun. He has outlived his own reputation for cruelty. He has outlived, he sometimes thinks, the need for any reputation at all. What remains is a pen, a lamp, and a stubborn conviction that the world makes sense if only you add it up correctly.

This morning it does not add up.

"Two million, nine hundred and four thousand, one hundred and twelve," he says aloud, to the empty room.

The ledger does not answer. It lies open on the desk before him, a vast gray-green book bound in cloth, its columns ruled in red. It is the Roll of the Refused, the register of every sleeper who heard the covenant read and said no. It is the oldest document in the Hall. It was Kuang's life's work, and Hai Ren's after him, and for the last fifteen years it has been Cheng Hui's, because nobody else could bear to read it.

He turns a page.

Two million, nine hundred and four thousand, one hundred and twelve.

At the head of the column, in his own neat hand, is a number he wrote on the first of the month. It is a smaller number. It is smaller by eleven.

He frowns.

He turns the page again, and runs a finger down the margin, and checks the sum. It is correct. He checks it a second time. It is correct again. He picks up the pen and writes, in the margin, with the care of a man defusing a trap: eleven absent, as of dawn.

Then he sets the pen down, and looks at the door, and thinks, quite calmly: I had better go and see.

---

The sleeping galleries of the Hall run for miles.

He has walked them every day for fifteen years, and he has never grown used to it. They are not corridors but caverns, vast vaulted halls with ceilings lost in shadow, and in every one of them, row on row on silent row, the sleepers lie. Their cots are narrow and white. Their blankets are folded at the foot. They lie with their faces turned up and their hands at their sides, in a stillness so absolute that after a while one stops seeing them as people and sees them as a kind of landscape, a field of pale wheat under a still sky.

He walks the east gallery quickly, with his lamp held high.

He passes the bronze lamp that Hai Ren once told him a boy called Pebble would look for. He passes a row of children, ten abreast, with their small hands curled like shells. He passes an old man with a beard to his waist, and a girl with a scar across her forehead, and a woman in the rags of a soldier's cloak. He counts without meaning to. It is a habit. Three hundred and four. Three hundred and five.

At the end of the gallery there is a gap.

It is not large. It is a single cot, empty, with the blanket turned back and a pillow still dented in the shape of a head. The cot beside it is empty too. And the one beyond. He stops. He lifts the lamp, and the light runs along the row, and he sees them: eleven narrow white beds, side by side, each as vacant as a mouth.

He stands very still.

On the nearest cot, on the folded blanket, there is a small flat card. It is a plain square of gray paper. He knows it at once. It is a Roll card, the kind the clerks pin to the head of every sleeper's bed: a name, a date, a tick in a box. This one has been taken down. Someone has turned it over and written on the back.

He reads it.

Gone up. Do not follow. It is kind.

It is not signed.

---

"It's not a hoax," says Hai Ren.

She is seventy-six years old, and she has the look of a sergeant who has seen the sky fall too many times to bother ducking. She is short, broad, and spare, with a square brown face and a cropped white head, and she wears the gray tunic of the Hall's registrar with a patched elbow and a stain on one cuff. She stands in the east gallery with her arms folded, glaring at the eleven empty cots as though she could shame them into refilling.

"I know it's not a hoax," says Cheng Hui.

"I'm saying so before you do."

"You are very kind."

"I'm not." She turns her glare on him. "I've had four reports since dawn. Four. Six cots in the south gallery. Nine in the west. Fourteen in the old vault, where nobody's been since the war. Forty-one, so far, and the day is young."

"Forty-one."

"And I haven't had a report from the lower levels yet. The low galleries are dark. We don't walk them every day."

Cheng Hui closes his eyes.

He does the sum without effort. It is not a hard one. Forty-one in the morning. Rising. The curve of the first hour is always the gentlest. He sees, with the cold precision of his trade, a line on a page, climbing. He sees it pass a hundred, a thousand. He sees it bend.

"They are leaving at an accelerating rate," he says.

"Obviously."

"And no one has seen them go."

"Nobody sees anything. That's the trouble." Hai Ren rubs her face. "The night watch swears they never left their posts. The doors are barred. The guards at the gate say not a soul went by. These people just—" She makes a vague gesture. "—stood up and walked into the dark."

"Perrin Ado," says Cheng Hui.

She looks at him.

"He woke with a voice, you recall. A loved voice, calling him by a name no one living had heard." He opens his eyes. "He said it asked for nothing. He said it said, Is that enough? And another answered, No. Keep going."

"I remember."

"Where is he?"

Hai Ren's face goes very still.

"I'll find out," she says.

---

They find him in the chapel.

It is a small plain room at the head of the east stair, used for weddings and funerals and the occasional furious argument. There is a stone altar, a bank of candles, a row of wooden benches worn smooth by generations of bottoms. Perrin Ado is sitting on the front bench with his hands folded in his lap and a look of mild contentment on his face. He is eighty-eight, and frail, and he wears a robe so patched that it has become a kind of quilt.

He looks up as they enter.

"Ah," he says. "Master Cheng. Madam Hai. I was hoping it would be you."

"Perrin." Cheng Hui crosses the floor. "You are well?"

"I am very well." The old archivist beams. "I am better than I have been in years. I have been sitting here since the fourth bell, listening to the most remarkable music."

"Music."

"Not the kind you hear." His eyes are bright and a little unfocused. "It is a voice. A great many voices, really, all singing the same note. They are very far away. They are calling me, and I think—" He tilts his head, as at a distant sound. "I think I should go."

"Go where?"

"North. Up the stair." He smiles. "It is a long way, but I am told it is quite easy. One simply walks."

Hai Ren has gone white.

"Perrin," she says, very low. "Who told you?"

"My wife."

"Your wife is dead."

"Yes, dear, I know." His voice is unperturbed. "But she is also up the stair. She is waiting for me. She has been waiting for six hundred years, and she has made porridge." He lays his hands on his knees. "Isn't that lovely?"

Cheng Hui kneels.

He does it slowly, with a crack of old joints, and takes the archivist's thin hands in his own. They are cold. They are trembling, very slightly, like leaves. He looks into the faded gentle brown eyes, and what he sees there is not madness, not fear, not even confusion. It is peace, a vast, soft, bottomless peace, like the surface of a lake at dawn.

"Perrin," he says. "Listen to me. It is not your wife."

"I know."

"You know."

"Of course I know. I'm not a fool." The smile does not fade. "I told Mei of the Nine, years ago. I said, the voice asked for nothing. That is how you can tell." He pats Cheng Hui's hand. "But it is such a kind voice, Master Cheng. And I am so tired. And I think, if one is going to be fooled, it may as well be by someone who loves you."

"It does not love you."

"No." A sigh. "But it does a very good impression."

---

He tries for an hour.

He does everything a sensible man can do. He argues. He pleads. He quotes the Roll, the covenant, the oath of the Hall. He sends for Hai Ren's stoutest guards and has the door barred, and the old man sits on his bench in the candlelight with the same gentle smile and watches them with the polite interest of a guest at someone else's quarrel. At the end of the hour Perrin Ado rises, quite steadily, thanks them for their trouble, and walks to the door.

The guards do not stop him. Cheng Hui sees it happen, and cannot understand it. They simply step aside, as people step aside for a funeral, and the old man passes between them with his hands folded and his patched robe whispering over the stone.

"Stop him!" snaps Hai Ren.

"We can't, Madam," says the sergeant. His voice is thin and strange. "I'm sorry. I don't know why. I just—" He swallows. "It doesn't feel right. It feels like it would be rude."

Cheng Hui follows.

He cannot help it. He walks behind the archivist down the long corridor, past the lantern-lit niches, down the great stair into the central gallery, where the floor is crowded with cots and the light falls from the high windows in long gray bars. And he sees, as he reaches the foot of the stair, that Perrin Ado is no longer alone.

They are walking.

They are coming out of the galleries in ones and twos and threes, in the gray light of the morning, women and men and children, young and old, in the patched rags of two centuries. They walk without haste. They walk without talking. Their faces are turned toward the north door, and they wear the same soft, vacant, happy look, the look of people hearing a lullaby. There are forty. There are a hundred. There are, he sees, as the great doors swing open on their own and the cold morning pours in, more than he can count.

He stands at the foot of the stair with his lamp in his hand and watches them go.

They pass him one by one. Some of them nod to him, shyly, as one nods to a neighbor. A woman with a baby on her hip lifts a hand. A boy of ten gives him a wave. And at the end of the line, last of the first hundred, Perrin Ado stops, and turns, and says in his thin cheerful voice:

"Do come along, Master Cheng. It's quite all right. It's only a walk."

"No," says Cheng Hui.

"As you wish."

"I will not."

"Of course." The archivist inclines his head. "I only thought you would want to know. They're not going to the stair for pleasure."

Cheng Hui's mouth goes dry.

"What do you mean?"

"The voice told me." Perrin smiles apologetically. "It said that there had been a fire, and that the hours were gone, and that the Door needed replacing. It said it did not wish to take from the willing. It said it would only ask those who had already said no." He pats his chest. "It said we were the only ones who would not be missed."

The old man turns away.

He walks out of the Hall, through the great doors, into the gray morning, and the line closes behind him like a hand.

---

He rides out to the road at noon, because Hai Ren has forbidden it and because he has never in his life done a thing merely because it was allowed.

The north road is a river. He had known it would be, but the knowing does not prepare him. He reins in his old gray mare at the crest of the first hill, with a clerk on either side and a banner of the Hall furled across his saddle, and looks down on a sight that no living eye has seen. The road runs away to the horizon, six abreast, and on it, shoulder to shoulder, the Refused are walking. They walk in a silence so deep that he can hear the scuff of bare feet on packed earth, a soft continuous whisper like the sound of wind in a field of wheat. They have no packs. They have no water. Some of them are barefoot. Some are in their nightshirts. A small boy rides on the shoulders of a giant, and the giant is weeping, quietly, with a face of unbearable joy.

Tian Mo is standing in the middle of the road.

He has been standing there for four hours. His forty men are drawn up behind him in a double line, with their shields locked and their spears grounded, and the Refused part around them without a ripple, as a stream parts around a bridge pier. He has his sword in his hand. He has not used it. He is fifty-six years old, with a gray, weathered face and a scar through one eyebrow, and as Cheng Hui rides up he lifts his eyes and says, in a voice that is hoarse as a crow's:

"They won't be turned."

"I see that."

"I've tried everything. I've tried shouting. I've tried standing in front. I've tried asking them nicely." A bitter laugh. "I tried carrying one off over my shoulder. She didn't struggle. She just kept walking. In the air. With her feet off the ground."

Cheng Hui dismounts.

He does it stiffly, with a grunt, and stands beside the captain in the roadway while the river flows past. Close up, the faces are worse. They are smooth and vacant and very, very happy. They are the faces of children at a feast.

"There is a girl," says Tian Mo.

"A girl."

"Eight rows back. In the third file." His eyes are fixed on a point in the crowd. "She's about thirty. She's got a scar on her chin and a braid down to here. I thought—" He stops. "I've seen that face. I've seen it somewhere. And I couldn't think where, and then I did."

"Where?"

"On Pebble."

Cheng Hui goes very still.

"The boy who went up the Road," Tian Mo says. "With Yue. The one who asked me for a map of the Hall before he left, and found a bronze lamp, and stood behind it for an hour." His throat works. "He told me he had a sister. He said she was asleep. He said she'd said no. He described her to me so carefully that I could draw her."

"Sun."

"That's the name."

Before Cheng Hui can speak, Tian Mo has stepped into the flow. He moves like a man wading a ford, shoving through the rows with his shoulder, and the walkers part for him, courteously, without pausing, until he reaches the third file and the thin, brown, braided woman with the scar on her chin. He takes her by the arm.

She stops.

It is the first time anyone has seen one of them stop. She stands in the roadway, with the river flowing round her, and turns her head, and looks at him. Her eyes are wide and dark and perfectly clear. They are not vacant. They are, Cheng Hui sees with a cold shock, entirely, terribly sane.

"Sun," says Tian Mo. "Your name is Sun. Your brother is Pebble. He's alive. He's gone up the Road after you. He's looking for you in every gallery he can."

"I know," she says.

Her voice is low, and calm, and a little hoarse.

"Then why—"

"Because I want to." She smiles. It is a wry, wondering, human smile, and it makes Tian Mo's grip falter. "I said no. I thought I was afraid. I wasn't. I was angry. I thought I'd been robbed." She glances at the river, the thousands of heads, the sun on the road. "And then someone woke me this morning, in the dark, and said it was time. And it didn't feel like a trick. It felt like being asked."

"It is a trick—"

"I know that too." She touches his hand, gently. "I'm not a fool, Captain. I've had five hundred years to think. I know it's the Bloom. I know it wants the hours. I know it'll burn us."

"Then—"

"And I'm going anyway." She draws a breath. "Because it's the only way I'll ever get to the top. And when I get there, I'm going to find out what it's afraid of."

Tian Mo stares at her.

"Tell my brother I'm sorry," says Sun. "Tell him I said no, and then I said yes, and that I never meant to leave him."

She takes his hand off her arm, gently, the way a mother loosens a child's grip. Then she steps back into the flow, and the river closes over her, and she is lost in a moment among the thousands of bobbing heads.

Tian Mo stands very still.

"She knew," he says, at last. His voice cracks. "She knew all of it."

"Yes."

"And she went."

"Some of them know," says Cheng Hui, quietly. "I think that is what frightens me most."

---

By noon there are four thousand.

By dusk there are forty thousand. Hai Ren reports it from the roof of the east annex, where she has set up a lookout with a spyglass and a long-suffering clerk. She stands at the parapet with the glass pressed to her eye and her jaw set, and Cheng Hui, climbing the ladder beside her, sees that her hand is shaking.

"Tell me," he says.

"It's a river." Her voice is flat. "I can see the road from here. The north road. They're coming out of every gate. They're coming out of the lower galleries, out of the old vault, out of places I didn't know had doors. They're walking in rows, six abreast, up the hill, and there's no end to them." She lowers the glass. "They're not running. They're not even hurrying. They're just going. And every one of them is smiling."

"Where is the road?"

"North."

"To the Azure Cloud Sect."

"To the Hundred Stairs." She wipes her eyes with the back of a hand. "Tian Mo's gone after them with his men. He's trying to turn them. It's like trying to turn a flood with a sword. They don't fight. They just step round him. They're polite about it."

Cheng Hui takes the glass.

It is a long, bright, trembling image: the road, gray and winding under a bruised sky, and on it a ribbon of figures stretching to the horizon. They move as a single creature, a vast slow undulation of heads and shoulders, and above them, over the hills, the first stars are coming out. He lowers the glass.

"I must write to Mei," he says.

"Mei's at the Wall."

"Then I must write to the Wall."

"What will you say?"

He is silent for a long moment.

"That the Roll of the Refused is emptying," he says at last. "That the Door has found new hours. And that they are walking up the Road of Nine in their sleep." He folds the glass shut. "And that no one in this world will be able to stop them, because every one of them is going willingly."

"It's not willing," says Hai Ren, fiercely. "It's not. They've been tricked."

"They have been offered something they wanted."

"That's the same thing!"

"No," says Cheng Hui. "It is a great deal worse."

He stands at the parapet in the failing light, an old man with a spyglass and a pen, and watches the river of the willing climb the hill toward the stair. And he thinks of the number in the ledger, which he can no longer make add up: two million, nine hundred and four thousand, one hundred and twelve. He thinks of the covenant, the promise, the oath. He thinks of a young man who walked up this road once with a machine in his head and a lie on his lips, and of what that young man would say, if he could see this.

Every advantage has a named cost.

He picks up his pen.

---

The letter takes him all night.

He writes it in the east annex, by the light of a single lamp, in a neat exact hand that does not shake. He sets down the numbers, the dates, the names. He sets down Perrin Ado's last words. He sets down his own conclusion, and then, because he is an honest man, he sets down the part he does not believe.

It may not be the Bloom, he writes. It may be something kinder. It may be that these two million wish to climb. That they have been waiting for permission. That the covenant was a door, and they have found the key.

He reads it over.

He crosses it out.

It is the Bloom, he writes instead, and it has just discovered that it does not need to fight.

He signs it. He seals it. He gives it to the courier at the first bell, a boy of sixteen on a lathered horse, and watches him ride north into the gray dawn. Then he goes to the window, and looks out at the road, and sees, to his surprise, that the river is not alone.

Something is walking against it.

It is a single figure, small, on foot, coming down the north road toward the Hall. It is moving steadily against the tide, in a gray robe too long for it, and the walkers part around it as a stream parts around a stone. He squints. He cannot make out the face. But he sees, as it comes up the last long hill into the light, that it is a child. A girl of nine or ten, with tangled dark hair and a cloak too big for her, holding something small and white to her chest.

She stops at the gate.

She looks up at the window where he stands. And Cheng Hui, who has been exact about everything for eighty-three years, finds that he has no idea what she is, or what she wants, or why he knows her face at once, though he has never seen it.

Sera, he thinks.

The girl lifts the white bell, and rings it once.

The sound goes through the Hall like a knife.
